cards.front: What is a network protocol, and why is one needed?
cards.back: An agreed set of rules defining the format, ordering, addressing and error handling of messages, so that devices made by different manufacturers can exchange data and interpret it in the same way.

keyPoints.text: governing the format or ordering of messages

cards.explanation: Without a shared protocol, two devices could both transmit correctly and still understand nothing.

cards.front: State what TCP and IP each do in the TCP/IP suite.
cards.back: TCP splits data into numbered packets, ensures reliable delivery, requests retransmission of anything lost and reassembles the packets in order. IP addresses each packet and routes it across networks towards its destination.

keyPoints.text: TCP handles reliable delivery and reassembly

mcq.correct: TCP splits data into numbered packets, ensures reliable delivery, requests retransmission of anything lost and reassembles the packets in order. IP addresses each packet and routes it across networks towards its destination.
distractors: TCP routes packets and IP guarantees delivery
TCP encrypts packets and IP compresses them
Both TCP and IP are concerned only with physical cabling

cards.explanation: IP alone is best effort and can drop or reorder packets; TCP is the layer that makes a byte stream reliable on top of it.

cards.front: What is the difference between circuit switching and packet switching?
cards.back: Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path with fixed bandwidth for the whole session. Packet switching splits data into packets that travel independently, possibly by different routes, and share bandwidth with other traffic.

keyPoints.text: circuit switching reserves a dedicated path

cards.explanation: Packet switching makes better use of a shared network and survives a link failure, at the cost of variable delay and the need to reassemble.

cards.front: What does the Domain Name System do?
cards.back: It translates a human-readable domain name into the IP address needed to route traffic, using a hierarchy of name servers so no single server has to hold every record.

keyPoints.text: translates a domain name into an IP address

cards.explanation: The hierarchy matters: a local resolver asks a root server, then the top-level domain server, then the authoritative server, caching answers along the way.

cards.front: A packet carries a source address, a destination address, a sequence number and a checksum. What is each for?
cards.back: The destination address lets it be routed, the source address lets a reply be sent back, the sequence number lets the receiver reorder packets that arrived out of order and spot missing ones, and the checksum lets it detect corruption in transit.

keyPoints.text: source address so a reply can be sent
sequence number to reorder and detect missing packets

cards.explanation: Each field answers a different failure of a best-effort network: where to send it, who sent it, what order it belongs in, and whether it arrived intact.

cards.front: What does HTTPS add to HTTP, and how does a browser know a site's certificate is genuine?
cards.back: It adds TLS encryption and server authentication. The browser checks the certificate's digital signature against a certificate authority it already trusts.

keyPoints.text: encryption of the data in transit

synonyms: the site is who it claims to be

keyPoints.text: the certificate is signed by a trusted certificate authority

mcq.correct: TLS encryption plus a CA-signed certificate
distractors: Only faster transfer using compression
A different port number, with no cryptographic change
A username and password sent with every request

cards.explanation: The encryption stops eavesdropping and the certificate stops impersonation; both are needed, since encrypting a conversation with an attacker is worthless. Trust works as a chain: the browser ships with a list of root CAs, and each certificate is verified back to one of them. A self-signed certificate encrypts perfectly well but cannot prove who is at the other end.

cards.front: Name the four layers of the TCP/IP model and say what each is responsible for.
cards.back: Application (the protocol the program uses, such as HTTP), transport (TCP or UDP, ports and reliability), internet (IP, addressing and routing) and network interface (the physical transmission).

distractors: Physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application
Hardware, software, protocol, application
Client, server, router, switch

cards.explanation: The second option is the seven-layer OSI model, which is the standard confusion: TCP/IP collapses OSI's presentation and session layers into application and its physical and data link layers into network interface. Each layer only talks to the layer directly above and below, which is what makes protocols replaceable independently.

cards.front: What is the difference between an IP address and a MAC address?
cards.back: An IP address is a logical address assigned to a network location and can change; a MAC address is a physical address built into the network card and is intended to be permanent.

keyPoints.text: an IP address is logical and can change
a MAC address is physical and fixed to the hardware
IP works across networks and MAC only within one
synonyms: MAC is local to the segment

mcq.correct: IP is logical and changeable; MAC is physical and fixed to the hardware
distractors: IP is physical; MAC is logical
Both are physical, but IP is longer
Both are assigned by the router and both can change

cards.explanation: A device keeps its MAC address wherever it goes but gets a new IP address on each network it joins. The two are tied together on a local segment by ARP, which resolves an IP address into the MAC address needed to actually deliver the frame. Routers work at IP level and switches at MAC level, which is why they do different jobs.

cards.back: In client-server a central server holds the data and serves requests, giving easy backup and central security but a single point of failure. In peer-to-peer each machine shares its own resources, which is cheap and has no single point of failure but is harder to secure and back up.

synonyms: a dedicated machine holds the data

keyPoints.text: peer-to-peer shares resources between the machines themselves
client-server gives centralised backup and security
peer-to-peer has no single point of failure

mcq.correct: Client-server centralises and is easier to secure; P2P is resilient and cheaper
distractors: Client-server is cheaper and more resilient; P2P is easier to secure
Client-server needs no server hardware
P2P requires a dedicated central machine

cards.explanation: The trade-off is control against resilience. A client-server network can enforce one security policy and take one backup, but if the server fails everyone stops working. A peer-to-peer network keeps working when any one machine fails, but security settings and backups are scattered across every machine - which is why businesses use client-server and small groups often do not.

cards.front: What does a router do that a switch does not?
cards.back: A router connects different networks and forwards packets between them using IP addresses; a switch connects devices within one network and forwards frames using MAC addresses.

keyPoints.text: a switch works within one network
synonyms: connects devices on the same segment
decides which network to send to next

mcq.correct: A router forwards between networks by IP; a switch forwards within one by MAC
distractors: A switch forwards between networks by IP; a router forwards within one by MAC
A router amplifies the signal; a switch stores files
They do the same job at different speeds

cards.explanation: A switch learns which MAC address is reachable on each of its ports and only sends a frame where it needs to go, replacing a hub that broadcast to everything. A router reads the destination IP address and works out which network to send the packet to next, which is what makes the internet possible. Devices can combine both, which is what a home router does.

cards.front: What are SMTP, POP3 and IMAP each used for?
cards.back: SMTP sends mail from a client to a server and between servers. POP3 downloads mail to the device and normally deletes it from the server. IMAP leaves mail on the server and synchronises it across devices.

keyPoints.text: POP3 downloads and usually deletes from the server
IMAP keeps mail on the server

mcq.correct: SMTP sends, POP3 downloads and deletes, IMAP synchronises on the server
distractors: SMTP receives, POP3 sends, IMAP encrypts
All three send mail, at different speeds
SMTP sends, POP3 and IMAP both delete mail immediately

cards.explanation: The difference that matters in practice is between POP3 and IMAP: POP3 suits one device and limited storage, while IMAP is what makes mail look the same on a phone and a laptop, because the copies live on the server. SMTP is used for both stages of sending - client to server and server to server - and never for collecting mail.

cards.front: Why can packets from one message arrive out of order, and how is the message still reconstructed?
cards.back: Each packet is routed independently, so they may take different paths of different length. Each carries a sequence number, and the receiving transport layer reorders them before passing the data up.

mcq.correct: Independent routing; sequence numbers allow reassembly
distractors: Packets are always in order; the file system sorts them
The router buffers all packets until the last one arrives
Out-of-order packets are discarded and the message is resent

cards.explanation: Packet switching deliberately lets each packet find its own way, which is what makes the network resilient to a failed link - but it means arrival order is not guaranteed. TCP puts them back in order, retransmits any that are missing and only then hands the byte stream to the application. UDP does none of this, which is why it is used where being late is worse than being wrong.
